newsitem.title: JAPAN: New Japan party to face pressure to join old guard.
newsitem.headline: New Japan party to face pressure to join old guard.

text.p: A new party led by baby boomers who want to breathe fresh life into Japan's staid politics emerged from Sunday's elections as a possible player in forming a government -- with the old guard it earlier attacked.

The Democratic Party was projected in television exit polls to win about 50 seats, enough to make its presence felt after polls in which the biggest party, the Liberal Democrats, fell short of a clear majority.

The Democrats were set to come in third behind Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's LDP, which was set to get 237 seats and Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) with 159, according to exit polls by Nippon Television.
LDP leaders have already said they will court the party led by Yukio Hatoyama and Naoto Kan.

Hatoyama, 49, and Kan, 50, who cobbled together the Democratic Party last month with the aim of creating an alternative to the LDP and Shinshinto, have in past weeks indicated they would go into opposition.
But Kan, who as health minister helped uncover a major scandal at his ministry over blood products tainted with HIV, has shown more interest in using the Democrats' clout in government than Hatoyama.
"We have never ruled out being part of the government," Kan said at party headquarters late on Sunday, adding that policy issues would determine the Democrats' stance toward the LDP.

The reformist Democratic Party could exact detailed policy promises before joining an LDP-led government, but runs the risk of serving mainly as a face-lift for the resurgent conservative party, analysts said.

Formed just weeks before the elections, the Democrats were launched with a vague platform and 52 rebel lawmakers from Sakigake and the Social Democratic Party, both junior partners in the outgoing Hashimoto government.
The fledgling party got cash from Hatoyama, a wealthy third-generation politician whose grandfather helped found the LDP in 1955, and charisma from Kan.

Kan gained hero status as the health minister who earlier this year disclosed his ministry's role in covering up a tainted blood scandal in which some 2,000 haemophiliacs contracted HIV, the virus which causes AIDS.

Kan, whose independent streak struck a chord in a country that had grown distrustful of unelected administrators after a series of scandals, promised the same no-compromise approach to other agencies.

As members of a minority partner in Hashimoto's LDP-dominated coalition, Hatoyama and Kan said they grew impatient with the lack of interest in reform within the LDP, which they said was sliding back to secretive, collusive ways.
